newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss minister regrets offence at blackmail remark.
newsitem.headline: Swiss minister regrets offence at blackmail remark.

text.p: Switzerland's economics minister said he was sorry if he had offended families of Holocaust victims but repeated his view that it was not the right time to set up a compensation fund for Jews who might be entitled to money left in Swiss banks after World War Two.
Jean-Pascal Delamuraz stirred angry protest from an international Jewish group on Tuesday by describing as "blackmail" demands for quick compensation for Holocaust survivors and heirs.

He said in a statement issued late on Thursday that he "regretted his remarks had been misunderstood and could have offended the feelings of the families of the victims of the abominable Holocaust," according to Swiss News Agency SDA.
Delamuraz's reference to blackmail, made while he was still president of Switzerland, was sharply criticised by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) and Israel's foreign ministry.
The WJC said in New York that Delamuraz had shown "shocking insensitivity". A spokesman for the Israeli foreign ministry had also said Israel regretted Delamuraz's remarks.

Special ambassador Thomas Borer told Reuters that while the spokesman for the Israeli foreign ministry had expressed regret over Delamuraz' remarks, he had also expressed satisfaction with the steps Switzerland has undertaken so far.
The WJC has proposed Switzerland set up a $250 million fund to compensate Holocaust survivors and heirs, who say Swiss banks have denied them money left there beyond the Nazis' reach.
In a newspaper interview Delamuraz also accused foreign critics of attacking Switzerland's role as a financial centre with accusations the Swiss profited cynically from the war.
The position of president of Switzerland rotates every year and on January 1, cabinet member Anold Koller assumed the post.
Delamuraz had said in the interview that cration of such a fund would be considered an admission of guilt by Switzerland.
Delamuraz repeated Berne's stance that any compensation should await the findings of a nine-member panel named two weeks ago to investigate the Swiss financial role in World War Two.

Berne has set up the nine-member panel of Swiss and international historians to report back in at most five years on the extent and fate of Jewish wealth and Nazi loot sent to neutral Switzerland during the war.
The panel has been empowered to lift Switzerland's strict banking secrecy laws in order to find the truth.

The commission is separate from an international panel set up by Swiss banks and world Jewish groups last May to search for individual lost Holocaust accounts and help return the assets to their rightful owners.
